title: The original one-neuron calculation
explain: Multiply corresponding inputs and weights, then add the bias. ReLU replaces the negative result with zero.

title: Four neurons sharing one input
explain: Each row defines a different neuron. The final column is its bias.
correction: The handwritten four-node picture writes 4 for the third output. Its printed weights give 0×2 + 1×1 + 1×3 + 1 = 5; the text in the collection also gives 5.

title: A complete two-layer network
explain: The second layer receives four hidden values. Biases are appended as a row of ones for the matrix calculation.

title: Process three examples together
explain: Examples are columns. The same parameters are reused for each example.

title: Follow seven layers
explain: The first six layers use ReLU; the final layer stays linear. No biases are shown in this exercise.
correction: Applying ReLU to the final layer would erase its negative outputs and change the exercise.

title: Route two tokens to different experts
explain: Column one selects expert two; column two selects expert one. Expert outputs then pass through ReLU.

title: A recurrent network across four inputs
explain: The same A, B and C are reused at each step. ReLU is applied to the hidden state.

title: Input-dependent state updates
explain: Here the exercise changes A, B and C between positions. The recurrence has no nonlinear activation.
correction: This describes the supplied toy recurrence, not a complete Mamba implementation.

title: The original matrix product
explain: A 2×2 matrix multiplies a 2×3 matrix to give a 2×3 result.

title: Sample “how are you” from the original probabilities
explain: The drawing accumulates probabilities from the bottom of its vocabulary list. Reversing the order into an ordinary cumulative list preserves its interval convention.

blocks.label: Probabilities, one row per generated position

correction: The probabilities are supplied to illustrate sampling; they are not calculated from a real language model in the exercise. Each row sums to one.

title: A three-layer perceptron with mixed activations
explain: The middle layer has no bias; the first and last do. A sigmoid is applied independently to the five final scores.
correction: Independent sigmoid outputs need not sum to one; use softmax when a single categorical distribution is intended.

title: Backpropagate through the original three layers
explain: Use softmax and cross-entropy with target [0,1,0]. The original sketch rounds the third class probability to zero; these gradients retain it.
correction: Rounded [0.5,0.5,0] probabilities are a teaching approximation. The exact logits [3,3,−1] give a small positive third probability; gradients change accordingly.

title: A position-wise feed-forward block
explain: The exercise supplies an attention mixing matrix, then applies the same feed-forward weights at each position.
correction: The supplied columns sum to two, not one. This is an unnormalized mixing example, not a softmax attention matrix or a full transformer block.

title: Normalize the original four-example batch
explain: Statistics are computed separately for each feature across the batch. This reconstruction uses population variance plus ε = 0.00001.
correction: The drawing rounds means and variances to integers. Exact means are [2.25,1.25,1.75], so its rounded normalization does not produce exactly zero mean and unit variance.

title: Calculate the original GAN forward pass
explain: The generator turns four noise examples into four fake examples. A shared discriminator scores both real and fake examples.
correction: For binary cross-entropy the logit gradient is prediction minus target before reduction. Rounded sigmoid values in the drawing are not exact probabilities.

title: Exact attention from the four-position exercise
explain: Examples are columns here. Normalize each query column of KᵀQ, then multiply V by those weights.
correction: The source replaces division by √3 with a floor-based shortcut and exp(x) with powers of three, then rounds again. Those approximations can substantially change the output; this table uses the exact stated attention formula.

title: Trace two dropout masks
explain: The first mask keeps units one and three at p=1/2. The second keeps units one and two at p=1/3. These are fixed sampled masks, not a deterministic rule.

blocks.label: Mean-squared-error gradient over all four entries

correction: The source uses 2(Y−target), which is the gradient of a sum of squared errors. Mean squared error over four entries divides that by four. Its approximate p=0.33 and scale 1.5 are made exact here by stating p=1/3. The separate evaluation panel uses altered illustrative weights; it is not the result of a calculated optimizer update from the training panel.

title: Reconstruct four examples with an autoencoder
explain: The two-dimensional bottleneck is decoded back into four dimensions. Targets equal the original inputs.
correction: A drawing of 2(Y−target) represents a sum-of-squares gradient. Averaging over all sixteen entries divides it by sixteen.

title: Rank the original three sentence vectors
explain: After the toy encoder, pooling and projection, rank candidates by raw dot product. These supplied projected vectors are enough to reproduce retrieval.
correction: The result selects “who am I” among the three supplied sentences. Projection is not required by all vector indexes, and raw dot product is not cosine similarity.

title: Contrastive scores for three text–image pairs
explain: Use the projected vectors shown in the source to compute all nine pairwise similarities. Normalize rows for image-to-text and columns for text-to-image.
correction: The source rounds pooling values, substitutes powers of three for exponentials and rounds probabilities. The reconstruction starts from its displayed projected vectors and uses actual exponentials. It does not claim the preceding rounded encoders are exact CLIP.

title: The original residual block
explain: Apply two affine maps and add the untouched input before the last ReLU.

blocks.label: FFN plus residual with toy ReLU

correction: The accompanying transformer drawing omits normalization and uses a supplied unnormalized mixing matrix. Its concept is residual addition; it is not a complete standard encoder.

title: Two rounds of graph aggregation
explain: Node features are columns; adjacency includes self-loops. Each round transforms node features and sums messages with the displayed adjacency.
correction: This is an unnormalized message-summing example. Normalized graph convolutions use a different operator. The tables are recalculated from the printed parameters rather than trusting handwritten intermediate values.

title: The diffusion sketch’s noise-prediction calculation
explain: The source takes encoded patches, adds supplied noise, applies a conditioning transform and mixes positions before predicting noise.

blocks.label: Noise-prediction MSE gradient over eight entries

correction: This toy arithmetic does not reproduce a commercial video system. The source’s one-step subtraction and rounded loss gradients are not a general diffusion sampling algorithm.

title: Route five mixed token vectors
explain: The displayed top-one gate scores select experts A, C, C, B and C. Expert C has capacity two, so the fifth token follows the exercise’s residual bypass policy.
correction: The original output writes [2,3,4] for the bypassed fifth token, but its input is [5,3,1]. An unchanged bypass must preserve [5,3,1]; the table corrects that inconsistency. Routing scaling omitted by the original is not inferred.

title: Reproduce the reward gap precisely
explain: The reward model assigns scores 3 and 5 to a declared rejected/preferred pair. Learning the comparison is separate from optimizing the language-model policy.

blocks.label: Vocabulary scores in order: him, her, them, is/are, doc, CEO

correction: The source’s 0.9 and −0.1 are rounded. A preference label is a judgment under specified criteria, not an objective proof of unbiased language or truth. The printed reward model gives 3 for the rejected pair and 4 for the preferred pair. The preferred first pooled feature is 4/3, but the source writes 5/3, producing its displayed reward of 5. The assumed-score example above uses [3,5]; the recomputed printed model instead has a gap of 1.
